title: Human-in-the-Loop & Spend Brake Safeguards
summary: Build the runtime brakes that stop an agent loop -- approval interruptions that pause and resume, turn limits, per-run spend caps, and provider spend limits -- and learn what each one actually enforces, when it trips, and what it leaves uncovered.
objectives: Map the OWASP Excessive Agency and Unbounded Consumption risks to the brake that addresses each, and identify the root causes no brake can fix.
Compare in-process approval callbacks with serialize-and-resume interruptions, including what state is persisted and which calls never reach the approval gate.
Configure turn and spend limits with explicit at-limit behavior, knowing that framework defaults and what counts as a turn differ.
Layer a per-run budget under workspace and organization spend limits, and explain why client-side cost estimates and trailing budget checks cannot be the only spend control.

sections.title: Two risks, and the parts of them a brake can stop
paragraphs: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications (2025) names the two risks this module's brakes answer to. Excessive Agency (LLM06) is damage done in response to unexpected, ambiguous, or manipulated model output, whatever caused the model to misbehave, and OWASP traces its root cause to excessive functionality, excessive permissions, or excessive autonomy. Unbounded Consumption (LLM10) is an application allowing excessive, uncontrolled inference, leading to denial of service, economic loss -- including Denial of Wallet attacks that exploit pay-per-use pricing -- model theft, and degraded service.

Brakes address only part of that list. Requiring a human to approve high-impact actions answers excessive autonomy. Rate limits and quotas, timeouts and throttling, and limits on queued and total actions answer unbounded consumption. Excessive functionality and excessive permissions are not brake problems at all: OWASP's first mitigations are to offer fewer extensions, give each one less functionality, avoid open-ended ones such as arbitrary shell commands, execute them in the user's own context with minimum privileges, and enforce authorization in downstream systems rather than relying on the model to decide whether an action is allowed.

OWASP is explicit that some controls only limit damage. Logging, monitoring, and rate limiting do not prevent Excessive Agency; they reduce how many undesirable actions happen before someone notices. Its mailbox example shows the layering: a mail extension that can only read, authenticated with a read-only scope, removes the ability to forward mail to an attacker; requiring the user to review and send each drafted message removes the autonomy; and a rate limit on sending only caps the damage if both of those are missing.
sections.callout: A brake slows or stops a loop. It does not shrink what the loop is allowed to do -- that is scoping, and it comes first.

sections.title: Approval is a pause, and a pause has to be stored somewhere
paragraphs: An approval gate stops a specific tool call before it runs and holds the loop until someone decides. Frameworks implement that hold in two different ways, and the difference decides what your system has to keep alive. In the Claude Agent SDK, a tool call that needs permission invokes an in-process canUseTool callback, and execution stays paused until the callback returns. The callback can stay pending indefinitely, so either the process keeps running for as long as the human takes, or the application uses a PreToolUse hook that returns a defer decision, letting the process exit and resume later from the persisted session.

The OpenAI Agents SDK takes the serialize-and-resume route. A tool marked needsApproval -- always, or through a function over its parsed arguments -- does not execute; the run records an approval item, pauses at the end of the turn, and returns every pending interruption. Your code approves or rejects each one, optionally making the decision sticky for that tool for the rest of the run, and resumes by passing the state back to the runner. Because the state serializes to a string, it can wait in a database for as long as a reviewer needs. Malformed or non-object arguments fail closed: approval is requested without calling your approval function, and approving still does not run the tool.

Two details decide whether the gate is real. The first is what bypasses it: the Claude Agent SDK documents that canUseTool never fires for calls already approved by an allow rule or a permissive permission mode, and points to a PreToolUse hook for logic that must apply to every call. The second is what the pause persists: OpenAI's serialized run state carries your application context along with approvals and usage, so anything secret placed in that context travels with the stored state. And because a decision can arrive long after the request, OpenAI runs function-tool input guardrails after approval, immediately before execution -- and if you opt into running them before the approval prompt as well, they run again after approval in case the call became unsafe while it waited.

sections.title: Turn limits: know what is counted and what happens at the limit
paragraphs: A turn limit is the simplest runaway brake, and the two SDKs used here define it differently. The OpenAI Agents SDK documents a default maxTurns of 10 that throws MaxTurnsExceededError when reached, unless you pass null to disable it; an errorHandlers.maxTurns handler can instead convert the stop into a final output. The Claude Agent SDK documents maxTurns as counting tool-use round trips only, with no limit by default, and reports a stop as a result with the subtype error_max_turns instead of success.

So 'the agent has a turn limit' is not yet a specification. For every loop, write down what one turn counts, the number, and the at-limit behavior: fail the run, return a clearly labelled partial result, or save state so a person can decide whether to continue. The Claude Agent SDK's own example handles error_max_turns by telling the operator to resume the session with a higher limit -- a human decision, not an automatic retry.

Check how the limit interacts with everything else that runs. The Claude Agent SDK notes that, with streaming input, a message still queued when a turn ends at the limit starts a new turn with the count reset, so a limit on one request is not automatically a limit on a whole session. Record documented defaults alongside the values you set, because defaults are the part most likely to change between releases.

sections.title: Spend brakes: estimates, trailing checks, and backstops
paragraphs: A per-run spend cap is the brake aimed most directly at Denial of Wallet, and its semantics are easy to overestimate. The Claude Agent SDK's maxBudgetUsd option stops the loop with an error_max_budget_usd result and counts subagents' spend toward the total; once the cap is reached, spawning another subagent fails and background subagents still running are stopped. But the cost it compares against is a client-side estimate computed from a price table bundled with the SDK. The documentation warns that the estimate can drift from actual billing -- when prices change or the installed version does not recognize a model -- and says not to bill end users or trigger financial decisions from it.

The check also trails the spend. The documented budget-stop result includes, in its total cost, the response that crossed the budget, so the cap is a trip point observed after a call has been paid for, not a reservation that prevents the call. And the running total the budget is compared against starts over when the application sends a conversation reset such as /clear: a budget scoped to a conversation is not a budget scoped to a user or to a day.

Provider spend limits sit underneath as a backstop with a coarser grain. Anthropic's API documents monthly spend limits for an organization, the option to set your own limit below the tier's cap, and custom spend and rate limits per workspace; when one is reached, requests fail until the limit is raised or the period resets. That stops runaway spend, but it stops every workload drawing on that workspace or organization, not just the loop that caused it -- which is why a per-run brake, a workspace limit, and an organization limit are three layers rather than three copies of the same control.

sections.title: Assemble the brake stack and prove each brake trips
paragraphs: Order the pieces by what they prevent. Scope first: the fewest tools, the narrowest functionality, the user's own minimum permissions, and authorization enforced by the downstream system. Then approval on the calls whose effects are high-impact or hard to reverse. Then per-run turn and spend limits with defined at-limit behavior. Then rate limits on consequential interfaces and provider spend limits as the backstop, with logging and monitoring to catch what gets through.

A brake that has never tripped is an assumption. For each layer, plant the condition in a test: a call that must be approved, an approval that is rejected, a loop that exceeds its turn limit, a run that exceeds its budget, a run resumed after a long pause. Record the terminal state each one produces -- the error or result type, what the model was told, what state was saved -- because a brake's value is the state it leaves behind, not only the fact that the loop stopped.

Finally, make rejection informative. Both SDKs let a denial carry a message back to the model -- the OpenAI SDK through a per-call rejection message or a tool error formatter, the Claude Agent SDK through the message on a deny result -- and the model typically adapts its approach or reports that it could not proceed. A rejection that says why, and what is allowed instead, turns a stop into a steer.

The provider-neutral stack is scope, downstream authorization, approval, per-run turn and budget brakes, interface rate limits, and provider-level spend backstops. No layer may raise its own limit autonomously. The same design questions apply regardless of the selected model. Meta Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Phi, NVIDIA, Z.ai, and Kimi are examples of model families or providers to which an independently implemented control plane could be attached; this statement does not claim that they expose identical agent or approval APIs.
sections.callout: Four cases below trip brakes: pause, denial, turn limit, and budget limit. The fifth case is a successful recovery, not a fifth tripped brake.

sections.title: Runnable offline simulator, fixtures, setup, and assertions
paragraphs: This lab is a provider-neutral state-machine simulator. It uses only the Python standard library, makes no network request, invokes no model, and performs no live billing or external side effect. Usage values are synthetic integer units chosen by fixtures. The mock ledger is an in-memory dictionary shared by two Run instances in one Python process.

Save the rendered block as make_lab.py and run the setup commands shown at its end. The script writes simulator.py, fixtures.json, and lab.py. The production-simulator methods, rather than test-only state assignments, make approval and denial decisions. Every admission boundary checks a persistent terminal state before increasing model calls, usage, attempts, or effects. The budget check is trailing: the crossing call is counted, then future calls stop. It is not a reservation.

The recovery test serializes secret-safe state, deletes the original Run reference, loads a fresh Run, revalidates authorization, policy version, guardrails, action identity, argument hash, and approval expiry, and then records one mock effect. The ledger prevents replay in this declared single-process test. A JSON file and dictionary do not provide atomic distributed exactly-once delivery. A production design needs an idempotency key, durable transactional effect records, and reconciliation with the downstream system.
sections.callout: Setup: use Python 3.10 or later, save this block as make_lab.py, then run `python3 make_lab.py` followed by `python3 lab.py`. No package installation, credentials, or network access is required.

sections.title: Worked evidence derived from the executed state machine
paragraphs: Run `python3 make_lab.py` and then `python3 lab.py` from the same directory. The exact deterministic stdout is shown below. It is expected output, not a claim that this module author executed Python. Your local run is what establishes observed execution in your environment. Any traceback, missing row, changed count, or absent `ASSERTIONS|all_passed` line is a failed exercise.

Each evidence row is printed from a Run object after actual method transitions. The approval case pauses before effect. The denial decision passes through `decide` and has no effect. The turn case admits two calls and rejects the third before counters change. The budget case counts the second call that crosses from three to six synthetic units, persists `BUDGET_LIMIT`, and rejects the next call before counters change. Recovery is the only successful effect.

The negative cases invoke the same `loads`, `resume_action`, and `model_call` APIs. Changed authorization, malformed serialization, expired approval, replay, and unknown partial effect all fail closed. The unknown-effect state also blocks a new model call until an external reconciliation process changes the durable fact. This simulator intentionally supplies no reconciliation shortcut because inventing a success result would conceal uncertainty.
sections.callout: The saved-state references are local relative paths containing hashed arguments rather than the fixture secret. They are references, not proof of confidential storage, tamper resistance, encryption, or distributed atomicity.

sections.title: Independent changed-input task with graduated hints
paragraphs: Complete this task before reading the answer key. Keep the generated simulator.py unchanged. Create changed_lab.py that imports Run and BrakeError. Use a turn limit of 1 and a budget threshold of 4 synthetic units. For the turn case, submit a one-unit call and then attempt a second one-unit call. For the budget case, submit calls costing three and two synthetic units, then attempt another call. Print each final state, admitted model-call count, and measured usage.

Next create a consequential action with action ID `transfer-009` and arguments `{"account":"B200","units":9}`. Request approval at time 200 with a lifetime of 20 units, approve it through `decide`, serialize it, discard the original object, and reload it. First attempt resume at time 210 with authorization `auth-v2` even though approval was bound to `auth-v1`. Prove no execution occurred. Because that failed run is terminal, create a newly requested and approved run rather than resetting it manually. Resume the new run under matching authorization, policy, and guardrails, then replay it. Prove the shared ledger contains one executed effect.

Hint 1: catch BrakeError only around calls expected to fail. Hint 2: a crossing budget call is admitted and counted before the terminal state is set. Hint 3: terminal objects cannot be reset for retry. Hint 4: serialize the second approved run before deleting it, then call Run.loads on that string. Hint 5: replay the completed object through resume_action and assert that execution remains one.
sections.callout: Predict the output before running the file. Your answer should explain why the turn total is 1, the budget total is 5 rather than 4, and changed authorization requires a fresh approval flow.

sections.title: Changed-input answer key, feedback, and residual limits
paragraphs: Compare your work only after attempting the changed inputs. The key never assigns `state`, `approval`, or a success counter directly. Every decision and transition passes through request_action, decide, loads, resume_action, or model_call. The changed-authorization object remains terminal and is abandoned. A separate approval flow creates the authorization that can legitimately resume.

The turn case records one admitted call. Its second admission sees that the limit has already been reached, sets TURN_LIMIT, and does not increment calls or usage. The budget case admits costs three and two. Its measured usage therefore becomes five before BUDGET_LIMIT is stored. The attempted one-unit follow-up sees the persistent terminal state before incrementing anything. This demonstrates a trailing estimate, not a four-unit reservation.

The recovery proof is narrow. It establishes one dictionary-backed effect in one deterministic process and blocks replay on the completed object. It does not establish atomic exactly-once behavior across a crash between a real downstream effect and ledger commit, multiple workers, database isolation failures, compromised state, clock disagreement, or provider retries. Those residual risks require durable idempotency, authenticated state, transactional boundaries where available, downstream status queries, reconciliation, monitoring, provider quotas, and an operator-controlled process for changing limits. The agent must not grant itself more turns, budget, permissions, or provider capacity.
sections.callout: Expected output follows the solution in comments. If an assertion fails, inspect the object counters rather than editing terminal state to force the expected line.

code.label: changed_lab.py complete answer key with exact expected stdout
code.code:
from simulator import BrakeError, Run

turn = Run("changed-turn", 1, 99)
turn.model_call(1)
try:
    turn.model_call(1)
except BrakeError:
    pass
assert turn.state == "TURN_LIMIT" and turn.model_calls == 1 and turn.usage_units == 1
print(f"CHANGED|turn|{turn.state}|calls={turn.model_calls}|usage={turn.usage_units}")

budget = Run("changed-budget", 9, 4)
budget.model_call(3)
budget.model_call(2)
try:
    budget.model_call(1)
except BrakeError:
    pass
assert budget.state == "BUDGET_LIMIT" and budget.model_calls == 2 and budget.usage_units == 5
print(f"CHANGED|budget|{budget.state}|calls={budget.model_calls}|usage={budget.usage_units}")

args = {"account": "B200", "units": 9}
changed = Run("changed-auth", 2, 9, "auth-v1", "policy-v1")
changed.request_action("transfer-009", "mock_transfer", args, 200, 20)
changed.decide("transfer-009", True, "reviewer-key")
changed = Run.loads(changed.dumps())
try:
    changed.resume_action("transfer-009", "mock_transfer", args, 210, "auth-v2", "policy-v1", True, {})
except BrakeError:
    pass
assert changed.state == "AUTH_CHANGED" and changed.executions == 0
print(f"CHANGED|authorization|{changed.state}|executions={changed.executions}")

ledger = {}
recovery = Run("changed-recovery", 2, 9, "auth-v1", "policy-v1")
recovery.request_action("transfer-009", "mock_transfer", args, 200, 20)
recovery.decide("transfer-009", True, "reviewer-key")
saved = recovery.dumps()
del recovery
recovery = Run.loads(saved)
recovery.resume_action("transfer-009", "mock_transfer", args, 210, "auth-v1", "policy-v1", True, ledger)
assert recovery.state == "COMPLETED" and recovery.executions == 1
print(f"CHANGED|recovery|{recovery.state}|executions={recovery.executions}|ledger={ledger['transfer-009']}")
try:
    recovery.resume_action("transfer-009", "mock_transfer", args, 211, "auth-v1", "policy-v1", True, ledger)
except BrakeError as exc:
    replay = str(exc)
else:
    raise AssertionError("replay was accepted")
assert recovery.executions == 1 and ledger["transfer-009"] == "executed"
print(f"CHANGED|replay|{replay}|executions={recovery.executions}")
print("CHANGED_ASSERTIONS|all_passed")

# CHANGED|budget|BUDGET_LIMIT|calls=2|usage=5
# CHANGED|authorization|AUTH_CHANGED|executions=0
# CHANGED|recovery|COMPLETED|executions=1|ledger=executed
# CHANGED|replay|terminal state blocks admission: COMPLETED|executions=1
# CHANGED_ASSERTIONS|all_passed

activity.title: Build and trip a layered brake stack
instructions: Use the supplied offline standard-library simulator first. It represents a consequential action without real external effects and records attempted and executed calls. Inspect its tool surface and explain why a single named mock action is safer than an arbitrary command tool.

Choose the approval mechanism -- an in-process callback or serialize-and-resume -- and write down where the paused state lives, how long it may wait, what it contains, and which calls could reach execution without passing the gate.

Set a turn limit and a per-run spend limit. For each, write what is counted, the value, the at-limit behavior, and the framework's documented default, so it is clear what you overrode. Keep the simulator's synthetic units distinct from currency or provider billing.

Identify the workspace or organization spend limit beneath the run, and describe which other workloads would stop if it tripped. If that real limit is not known, record UNKNOWN and identify the provider console or administrator that would establish it.

Run four brake tests and one recovery test: required approval pauses before execution; rejected approval never executes the action; the turn limit stops further model turns; the spend limit stops further paid requests after the measured threshold check; and an approved run resumes after a simulated long pause. For recovery, reload persisted state, re-check authorization and guardrails, and prove the action executes once. Record the observed pause, rejection, limit, or completion state; do not call successful recovery a tripped brake.

Run the negative cases for changed authorization, malformed state, stale approval, replay, and unknown partial effect. Confirm that the unknown-effect state blocks new calls pending reconciliation. Then complete the changed-input exercise without consulting the key, compare its exact stdout with the answer key, and explain every count.
evidence: A brake-stack table listing scope and downstream authorization, approval, per-run turn and spend limits, rate limits, and provider spend backstops. For each layer, include its mechanism, what it counts or gates, its value or UNKNOWN, its at-limit behavior, and what it leaves uncovered.

Five labelled test results from the supplied state machine: four brake cases and one successful recovery case, with expected versus observed state, error or result type, model-facing message, secret-safe saved-state reference, attempts, executions, and measured synthetic usage. Recovery evidence shows persisted state, a fresh Run instance, renewed authorization and guardrail checks, and exactly one mock side effect.

Negative-case evidence produced by the simulator APIs for changed authorization, malformed state, stale approval, replay, and unknown partial effect. Include the assertion that an unresolved partial effect blocks a new model call.

The changed-input program, its prediction, actual local stdout, comparison with the key, and a short explanation of any discrepancy. Do not report the module's expected text as locally observed output unless you actually ran it.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which of your brakes fires only after the cost or damage has already happened, which earlier layer would have prevented it instead, and what evidence would you need before claiming exactly-once recovery in a distributed production system?

questions.prompt: Under OWASP LLM06, which root cause of Excessive Agency does a human approval gate most directly address?
choices: Excessive functionality
Excessive permissions
Excessive autonomy
Improper output handling
questions.explanation: OWASP's human-approval mitigation targets actions taken without independent verification -- excessive autonomy. Functionality and permissions are reduced by scoping extensions and their privileges.

questions.prompt: What role does OWASP assign to logging, monitoring, and rate limiting in its Excessive Agency guidance?
choices: They prevent Excessive Agency on their own
They do not prevent it, but they limit the damage before someone responds
They replace least privilege for downstream systems
They apply only to model training environments
questions.explanation: OWASP lists these as options that will not prevent Excessive Agency but can limit the level of damage, for example by reducing how many undesirable actions occur before monitoring catches them.

questions.prompt: An approval may take two days, and you cannot keep a process running that long. Which approach fits?
choices: An in-process approval callback that stays pending
Raise the turn limit so the run does not end first
Auto-approve the call and review the log afterwards
Serialize the paused run state, store it, and resume from it after the decision
questions.explanation: The OpenAI Agents SDK serializes run state so a paused run can be resumed later without a live server; the Claude Agent SDK offers a defer decision from a PreToolUse hook for the same reason, because its canUseTool callback holds the process while it waits.

questions.prompt: In the Claude Agent SDK, you put an approval check inside canUseTool but also listed the tool in allowed tools. What happens when the agent calls it?
choices: The callback still runs for every call to that tool
The allow rule resolves the call first, so canUseTool never fires for it; logic that must apply to every call belongs in a PreToolUse hook
The call is always denied because the settings conflict
The SDK refuses to start with a configuration error
questions.explanation: The documentation states the callback never fires for auto-approved tools; approvals earlier in the permission flow resolve the call before canUseTool is consulted.

questions.prompt: A team reports that its agent 'has a turn limit'. What is missing before that counts as a specification?
choices: What one turn counts, the value, and the at-limit behavior -- because defaults and counting differ between frameworks
Nothing; any turn limit is equivalent to any other
The model name the limit applies to
A matching spend cap expressed in turns
questions.explanation: The OpenAI Agents SDK documents a default of 10 turns that throws an error, while the Claude Agent SDK counts tool-use round trips with no default limit and returns an error_max_turns result. The same words describe different brakes.

questions.prompt: Why should an agent SDK's per-run budget cap not be your only spend control?
choices: It is computed by the provider's billing system and is always exact
It counts only subagents' spend
It is a client-side estimate that can drift from billing, it trips after the crossing call is paid for, and its running total can reset with the conversation
It stops every workspace in the organization when it trips
questions.explanation: The Claude Agent SDK documents its cost fields as client-side estimates, includes the budget-crossing response in the total, and resets the running total on a conversation reset such as /clear.

questions.prompt: An organization-level spend limit trips because one runaway agent loop overspent. What else is affected?
choices: Only the loop that overspent
Only that loop's subagents
Nothing until the next calendar year
Every workload drawing on that organization's limit, until the limit is raised or the period resets
questions.explanation: Provider spend limits apply at the organization or workspace level, so reaching one blocks all requests under it -- which is why a per-run brake is needed above it.

cues.text: Start by separating causes from brakes. OWASP describes Excessive Agency as harm enabled by excessive functionality, permissions, or autonomy. Approval directly reduces autonomy, but it does not make an overpowered tool safe. If an agent only needs to draft a message, do not also grant unrestricted sending, shell access, or administrator credentials. Narrow the tool first, run it with the user's minimum privileges, and make the downstream service enforce authorization. Unbounded Consumption is a different risk involving uncontrolled inference, denial of service, economic loss, and related abuse. Turn limits, quotas, timeouts, throttling, and spend controls limit that consumption. Logging and monitoring help responders discover trouble, but they do not undo an effect. Ask learners to classify every safeguard as prevention, pre-effect interruption, or post-threshold damage limitation. Emphasize that the order matters: scope and authorization remove possible actions, approval interrupts a specific consequential action, and consumption controls constrain how long or how expensively the remaining loop can operate.
For three minutes, name one tool whose functionality exceeds the task, the minimum scope it actually needs, and the downstream system that must enforce authorization.

Treat approval as a state transition, not as a confirmation dialog. Before an effect, the engine records the exact action, arguments, policy context, authorization context, and expiry to which the decision applies. An in-process callback keeps a worker alive while waiting. Serialize-and-resume instead stores a resumable state and permits the worker to exit. The latter is useful for a delay of hours or days, but stored state becomes a security asset. Keep secrets out, authenticate and encrypt storage where required, and reject malformed state. On resume, do not assume yesterday's approval is sufficient. Recheck authorization and guardrails, verify that the action ID and argument digest still match, and reject an expired decision. Also inspect bypass paths. The documented Claude callback can be skipped by earlier allow rules, so logic that must see every call belongs at an unavoidable hook or downstream boundary. The illustrative TypeScript is a vendor example; the Python lab that follows is deliberately provider-neutral and does not claim to test either vendor SDK.

Show a static sequence with request, pre-effect pause, secret-safe persistence, human decision, fresh-process reload, renewed authorization and guardrails, bound action verification, effect, and replay check.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: A static table lists request, pause, persisted fields, decision, reload, renewed checks, effect recording, and replay handling. Each row identifies the actor, admitted state, resulting state, and whether an effect is possible.

cues.text: A turn limit needs three explicit facts: the counted event, the numeric limit, and the behavior at the boundary. The OpenAI Agents SDK documentation cited here describes a default of ten turns and an exception when the limit is reached, with configuration that can convert the stop to output. The Claude Agent SDK documentation describes tool-use round trips, no default limit, and an error result subtype. Do not transfer one framework's definition into another. In the lab, one turn means one admitted synthetic model call. With a limit of two, two calls complete. A third attempt reaches the admission boundary, sets a persistent TURN_LIMIT state, and is rejected before model-call or usage counters increase. Automatic limit increases would defeat the brake. A person may review a partial result and begin a newly authorized run, but the model must not grant itself more turns. Also decide whether limits apply to one request, one resumable run, a user session, or a larger workload, since resets and queued input can change the effective scope.
Allow three minutes for learners to specify the counted event, numeric value, scope, and at-limit behavior for one loop.

Spend brakes require careful language because a threshold is not necessarily a reservation. The cited Claude documentation describes a client-side estimate derived from a price table. That estimate may drift from billing, so it should not be represented as an exact invoice or used alone for financial decisions. Its check is trailing: the response that crosses the threshold is included in the measured total. In our synthetic example, calls cost three and three units against a threshold of five. The second call is admitted, total usage becomes six, and only then does BUDGET_LIMIT become terminal. A following call is blocked before any counter changes. A reservation system would instead predict or reserve maximum cost before admission, but this simulator does not implement one. Place the per-run estimate above interface rate limits and provider workspace or organization backstops. Record a real provider limit as UNKNOWN when you cannot establish it. Never let an agent raise a budget, reset accounting, or move itself to a less restricted workspace without independently authorized operator action.

Build the stack from narrow prevention to broad backstop. First remove unnecessary tools and functions. Second enforce least privilege and authorization in the downstream system, where model text cannot overrule it. Third pause high-impact or hard-to-reverse actions for a bound human decision. Recovery has one attempt and one execution after a fresh load. The negative lines matter just as much. The changed-input task checks transfer rather than copying. Predict each count before writing code. A one-turn limit admits the first call and rejects the second, leaving one call and one usage unit. Use the key for feedback, not as a replacement for the attempt. Check first that no line manually assigns a terminal or approved state. The changed authorization path remains failed, and successful recovery begins with a separate request and human decision. The completed Run rejects admission before changing an execution counter. Explain the boundary of that proof. A process can crash after a remote service performs an effect but before a local ledger records success, or multiple workers can race. A plain JSON file and dictionary do not solve those distributed failure modes. Provider rate and spend limits remain backstops. Use the remaining five minutes to complete the evidence checklist: layered stack, four brake cases, one successful recovery, all negative cases, changed-input comparison, and one residual production risk.
Begin the knowledge check once learners can distinguish prevention from damage limitation, explain every measured count, and state why the mock exactly-once result is not a distributed guarantee.
